judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1849, a bill about the youngest age a child can be charged with a crime. Maine now sets a youngest age for being charged as a juvenile. A child under 11 cannot be charged with a juvenile crime. The exception is murder, felony murder, or manslaughter, or an attempt at one of those, where no minimum age applies. The law also sends juveniles to juvenile court for any offense under Maine law, including hunting and driving offenses that used to go to adult court. The Maine House passed it 76-71 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1723, a bill about rent increases in manufactured housing communities. The owner of a manufactured housing community must give at least 90 days' written notice before raising lot rent or fees. Lot rent is what a homeowner pays for the ground their home sits on. The notice must state the increase in dollars and compare it to average rent and fees at similar communities nearby. If the increase runs more than 1 point above the region's rise in everyday prices, residents may ask for mediation, a meeting with a neutral third person. The Maine House passed it 78-67 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1145, a bill about residents' chance to buy their mobile home park. When the owner of a mobile home park plans to sell, the residents get a real chance to buy it first. The owner must mail a complete notice to every homeowner and to the state housing authority, and the residents' 60-day window to make an offer does not start until that notice is complete and received. The notice must give the price and terms, including a signed copy of any offer the owner is ready to accept. If the buyer plans to fold the park into an investment portfolio, the notice must give the terms for that park on its own. The Maine House passed it 81-64 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 2146, a bill about which vaccines the state buys in bulk. Maine buys vaccines in bulk through a state program and supplies them to doctors' offices. The board that picks which vaccines the program buys must now also weigh what the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend. Those recommendations count only if they keep or widen access, rest on scientific evidence, and are not meant to weaken federal immunization standards. The board may also ask the state to pay for children's vaccines, which the Legislature must approve. The Maine Senate passed it 23-10 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1519, a bill about who cleans up used electronic cigarettes. A company that sells electronic cigarettes in Maine must set up and pay for a program that collects used devices and disposes of them safely. A company may run the program on its own, together with other companies, or through a shared organization. The plan has to be approved by the state environmental agency. This was the final passage vote. The Maine House passed it 75-68 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1117, a bill about job training grants. Maine gives grants to preapprenticeship programs, which prepare people to enter a registered apprenticeship. The grants may now pay for child care, transportation, tools, safety gear, and other costs that would otherwise keep someone from taking part, as well as cash stipends. At least 51 percent of the grant money must go to programs with a track record of enrolling people from historically marginalized communities and moving them into apprenticeships. The Maine Senate passed it 24-8 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 785, a bill about tribal representation and taxes. The Mi'kmaq Nation may elect a representative to the Maine House of Representatives, beginning with the Legislature elected in November 2026. The Penobscot Nation, the Passamaquoddy Tribe, and the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians already have that right. The law also exempts from state income tax the wages the four nations pay their own tribal members, and it adjusts sales, use, and property tax rules on tribal land. The Maine Senate passed it 22-11 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1934, a bill about outdoor lighting and the night sky. Outdoor lighting paid for by the state must be shielded so the light points down rather than into the night sky, and it may not be bluer or brighter than the standards allow. Lighting for sports fields has its own limits on how far the light may spread. The rules do not apply where federal aviation or highway rules require something different, during emergencies, for road work, for historic-style fixtures, or at ski areas. This was the final passage vote. The Maine House passed it 74-72 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 911, a bill about ranked-choice elections when a candidate drops out. Maine uses ranked-choice voting in some elections, where voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If a candidate dies, is disqualified, or withdraws fewer than 70 days before such an election, the election still stays a ranked-choice election. The law also spells out how the count works in that situation. The Maine Senate passed it 21-13 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1730, a bill about small plug-in solar panels. Maine residents may plug a small solar panel or battery into an ordinary outlet to offset the electricity they use at home. A system qualifies if it sends no more than 1,200 watts and meets recognized safety certification. These small systems are excused from some of the requirements that apply to larger rooftop solar. This was the final passage vote. The Maine House passed it 79-65 and it became law.
